solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Reactionary new school lacking aspiration (6)

indicatorNotes.lacking: the school goes without its aspirate H

blocks.note: N = new
HARROW, the English public school, without its H (an aspirate, the breathed sound)

annotation.surface: A school that has given up on ambition and turned backward-looking.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Aspiration' reads as ambition, but in phonetics it is the breathy H sound, so the school simply loses its H. Harrow is a famous English boarding school.
annotation.definitionFit: Narrow-minded, and so reactionary: resistant to new ideas.

entries.clue: Greek agents about to acquire Times (5)

indicatorNotes.to acquire: the agents take the Times inside them

blocks.note: CIA, the American spy agency, turned round
T = time, so two of them for the plural

annotation.surface: Greek spies about to get hold of copies of a London newspaper.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Times' looks like the London newspaper, but in wordplay it is just the abbreviation for time, doubled for the plural.
annotation.definitionFit: Attic means of Attica, the region around Athens, hence Greek.

entries.clue: Restore ecstasy enjoyed by Hindu queen and consort (9)

indicatorNotes.enjoyed by: the ecstasy is held, possessed, by the queen

blocks.note: a rani is an Indian queen
E = the drug ecstasy, placed inside RANI to make R-E-ANI
a consort is a partner, a mate

annotation.surface: A royal couple in India enjoying an illicit high.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Enjoyed by' is a container signal: the thing enjoyed is held within the enjoyer.
annotation.definitionFit: To reanimate is to bring back to life, to restore.

entries.clue: Building material inventor left half abandoned (6)

indicatorNotes.half abandoned: LEFT loses half its letters, keeping LE

blocks.note: James Watt, Scottish engineer of the steam engine
LEFT with its second half dropped

annotation.surface: An inventor quitting a half-finished building project.
annotation.walkthrough: Wattle, woven sticks, is plastered with daub to make walls.
annotation.definitionFit: Wattle is interwoven rods used in building walls and fences.

entries.clue: Is one clever to welcome Conservative, it being civilised? (8)

blocks.note: the question 'Is one clever?' asked of oneself: AM I ABLE?
C = Conservative, going in after AMI

annotation.surface: Someone wondering whether being clever means making room for a Tory.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Is one clever' has to be rephrased in the first person as AM I ABLE; then C slips in to give AMI-C-ABLE.
annotation.definitionFit: Amicable means friendly and polite, civilised.

entries.clue: Book overseas trip (1,7,2,5)

blocks.note: E M Forster's 1924 novel
literally, a voyage to India

annotation.surface: An instruction to reserve a holiday abroad.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Book' looks like the verb 'reserve'; it is the noun, a novel's title.
annotation.definitionFit: The Forster novel's title literally describes a sea journey to India.

entries.clue: Free of sin, as some popes were (8)

blocks.note: blameless
a papal name, borne by thirteen popes

annotation.surface: A remark that only some popes were sinless.
annotation.walkthrough: The second half reads as a sly dig at papal morals; it means named, not virtuous.
annotation.definitionFit: Innocent means free of guilt or sin, and is a papal name.

entries.clue: Hate violent crime associated with men (5)

blocks.note: ABH = actual bodily harm, a British assault charge
OR = other ranks, soldiers who are not officers

annotation.surface: Loathing of violence committed by men.
annotation.walkthrough: ABH, actual bodily harm, is a British legal term for a mid-level assault.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, though the answer is the stronger word: loathing with a shudder rather than mere dislike.

entries.clue: A long way from lethargy, I suspect (5,4)

indicatorNotes.suspect: the letters are dubious, not to be trusted as they stand

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

annotation.surface: Someone guessing that they are far from sluggish.
annotation.walkthrough: 'I suspect' reads as a hedge, but 'suspect' is the anagram signal and I is part of the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: A light year is a unit of astronomical distance, so a long way.

entries.clue: Badly mistreat an old puffer? (5,5)

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

annotation.surface: Cruelty to an elderly smoker.
annotation.walkthrough: An 'old puffer' sounds like a wheezing pensioner; it is a locomotive, puffer being a child's word for one.
annotation.definitionFit: A steam train puffs smoke and is now old technology.

entries.clue: Husband that’s horrible — this chap? (4)

blocks.note: H = husband
the exclamation of disgust

annotation.surface: Someone recoiling at a nasty husband.
annotation.walkthrough: The dash turns the whole clue into a pointer: the chap is named by what comes before it.
annotation.definitionFit: Hugh is a man's name, so any chap could be him; the question mark admits it.

entries.clue: Warrior suffers, wrongly held (8)

indicatorNotes.held: something held is gripped from both sides, so ACHES wraps around ILL

blocks.note: aches = suffers
ill = wrongly, as in ill-judged

annotation.surface: A soldier in pain after being wrongfully detained.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Wrongly held' reads as false imprisonment; wrongly gives ILL and held puts it in ACH-ILL-ES.
annotation.definitionFit: Achilles was the Greek hero of the Trojan War.

entries.clue: Look after dilapidated vehicle going round sharp bend, perhaps (6)

blocks.note: a crate is an old banger of a car
a U-bend or U-turn is the sharpest bend

annotation.surface: An old car taking a hairpin bend, which needs looking after.
annotation.walkthrough: U sits inside CRATE: C-U-RATE. 'Perhaps' flags U as one example of a sharp bend.
annotation.definitionFit: To curate is to take care of a collection.

entries.clue: Old poems from the east, almost all augmented (4)

indicatorNotes.from the east: in an across clue, read right to left

blocks.note: ADDED without its final D

annotation.surface: A collection of ancient eastern verse, expanded nearly throughout.
annotation.walkthrough: 'From the east' suggests Oriental poetry; it means read from the right, and the Edda is Norse.
annotation.definitionFit: The Edda is a medieval Icelandic collection of Old Norse poems.

entries.clue: Mark of a poor reviewer, they say (9)

indicatorNotes.they say: what follows is heard, not spelt

blocks.note: a dire critic is a bad reviewer

annotation.surface: A low score given by an incompetent reviewer.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mark' looks like a grade from a critic; it is an accent mark on a letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A diacritic is a mark such as an accent or cedilla added to a letter.

entries.clue: Tough guy going round concealing dread (8)

indicatorNotes.round: to turn something round is to face it the other way, so the word is read backwards
indicatorNotes.concealing: the reversed word hides ANGST inside it

blocks.note: the blog parse takes going as REG, then reversed to GER
angst = existential dread

annotation.surface: A hard man on his rounds hiding his fear.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dread' is the existentialist's angst, the fear that comes with freedom. Even the Times for the Times blogger could not say why 'going' gives REG, so this is the clue's weak step.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose fit: a gangster is a violent criminal, and toughness goes with the job.

entries.clue: Doctor protects a bystander (9)

indicatorNotes.Doctor: to doctor is to tamper with

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

annotation.surface: A doctor shielding an onlooker.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' leads as a noun, the subject; it is a verb meaning tamper with.
annotation.definitionFit: A spectator watches without taking part, a bystander.

entries.clue: Message in TV broadcast having little weight (8)

indicatorNotes.broadcast: the word for TV is heard, not spelt

blocks.note: telly is British slang for television
a gram is a small unit of weight

annotation.surface: A trivial announcement on television.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Having little weight' reads as unimportant; it is simply the gram.
annotation.definitionFit: The category is the definition: a telegram is one kind of message, the kind once sent by wire.

entries.clue: What might offer illumination when in fix? (8)

indicatorNotes.in: 'when in fix' says the when-word sits inside the fix-word

blocks.note: to cement is to fix firmly
as = when, as in 'as I left'

annotation.surface: A question about what could shed light when you are in a jam.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In fix' reads as in a predicament; fix is CEMENT, holding AS: C-AS-EMENT.
annotation.definitionFit: A casement is a hinged window, which lets light in.

entries.clue: Noble old king, 50, beating a retreat (4)

indicatorNotes.beating a retreat: the L withdraws to the back of the word

blocks.note: King Lear of Shakespeare's play

annotation.surface: An aged monarch of fifty in retreat.
annotation.walkthrough: '50' is not extra letters: it names the L already at the front of LEAR (L is 50 in Roman numerals), and that L retreats to the back.
annotation.definitionFit: Noble works as a noun here, a peer, and an earl is one rank of the British peerage.

entries.clue: Inquisitor in call for truce on island (6)

blocks.note: pax is a schoolchild's cry for a truce
the Isle of Man

annotation.surface: Someone on an island calling for a ceasefire.
annotation.walkthrough: Jeremy Paxman is a British TV interviewer famous for grilling politicians.
annotation.definitionFit: Paxman made his name as a relentless questioner on Newsnight.

entries.clue: Make a fuss about judge dropping an E (6)

indicatorNotes.dropping: an E is dropped into the judge word

blocks.note: C = circa, about
to rate is to judge
dropped in after R: R-E-ATE

annotation.surface: Complaining about a judge who lost a letter.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dropping' looks like losing the E, but the E is dropped in; create is British for kick up a fuss.
annotation.definitionFit: A British informal sense: to 'create' without an object means to kick up a row.

entries.clue: Abused Cockney ready to explode (5)

indicatorNotes.Cockney: the Cockney accent is heard dropping initial H, so the word is as spoken by one

blocks.note: abused = harmed, said with a dropped H

annotation.surface: A mistreated Londoner about to lose their temper.
annotation.walkthrough: Cockney is the working-class East London accent, which drops initial H.
annotation.definitionFit: A bomb's sense: once its fuse is set it is primed to go off, which is a narrower meaning than carrying weapons.

entries.clue: Around island, I cannot shake inertia (8)

indicatorNotes.Around: the shaken letters go around the island
indicatorNotes.shake: the letters of I CANNOT are shaken up

blocks.note: I = island
anagram fodder, 7 letters, arranged around I

annotation.surface: Someone stuck on an island unable to get going.
annotation.walkthrough: The complaint of being unable to shake off inertia is the definition's own feeling.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the everyday sense of inertia, sluggishness, not the physicist's resistance to change of motion.

entries.clue: Joke about weight taken the wrong way — toxic stuff! (5)

indicatorNotes.taken the wrong way: going the wrong way means travelling backwards, so the weight is read right to left

blocks.note: a joke is 'one', as in 'have you heard the one about...'
OZ = ounce, reversed

annotation.surface: A joke about weight misunderstood and causing offence.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Taken the wrong way' reads as offence; it reverses OZ, which sits inside ONE: O-ZO-NE.
annotation.definitionFit: Ozone is a poisonous form of oxygen at ground level.

entries.clue: A clever remark backfiring a bit? (4)

blocks.note: as written
MOT, as in bon mot, reversed

annotation.surface: A witticism that goes slightly wrong.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A bit' looks like a modifier; it is the definition, an atom being a tiny bit.
annotation.definitionFit: An atom is a tiny particle, the smallest bit of something.

entries.clue: Rescue men I deport in error (10)

indicatorNotes.in error: the letters are mistaken, out of place

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters

annotation.surface: An immigration official admitting a mistake and asking to save the men they expelled.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rescue' reads as a command; it is the noun.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, with a religious echo: redemption is being saved, from sin or from a plight.

entries.clue: A rebel soldier lost in scholarly setting (8)

blocks.note: as written
Jack Cade led a revolt in England in 1450
MIA = missing in action

annotation.surface: A rebel soldier who has gone missing among the dons.
annotation.walkthrough: Jack Cade led the 1450 Kentish rebellion, a stock crossword rebel.
annotation.definitionFit: Academia is the world of universities and scholarship.

entries.clue: Annoyed shopper starts to express dismay (6)

indicatorNotes.starts to: take the first letters of the next words

blocks.note: to shop someone is to inform on them; a nark is an informer
the first letters of express and dismay

annotation.surface: An irritated customer beginning to show disappointment.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Shopper' looks like a customer; it is British slang for an informer, one who shops people to the police.
annotation.definitionFit: A regional use: in British slang to be narked is to be irritated, and the answer shares its root with the informer.
